text: Support teams, spam filters and content moderators all do the same thing: read text and assign a label. You can already clean text and turn it into TF-IDF vectors. Now we train a classifier on those vectors.
Our data is sixty short, illustrative support tickets, twenty each labeled billing, bug and how-to. We split it with stratification, so all three classes appear in both train and test.
Then one scikit-learn pipeline chains TF-IDF to logistic regression. Because the vectorizer lives inside the pipeline, it learns its vocabulary from training text only.

On the held-out tickets, the model scores sixty-seven percent. A majority-class baseline scores thirty-three, so it learned something. Bug tickets have the weakest recall. But the test set has just fifteen tickets, five per class, and one ticket moves the score by about seven points. Treat this number as an anecdote.

Cross-validation gives a steadier picture. Five folds scored from sixty-seven to eighty-three percent, averaging seventy-eight. That spread is the real message: with sixty examples, you cannot tell a seventy-eight percent model from an eighty-two percent one. Removing stop words lowered the average to seventy, and a weaker regularization setting raised it to eighty, but both differences sit inside the noise.
Now look inside. This code plots each class's six strongest words.

Invoice, card and refund point to billing, and error and fails point to bugs, which makes sense. But my is the top billing word, simply because our sample happens to say my invoice a lot. And how, can and do define the how-to class, which is real signal, and that is why removing stop words hurt. Reading coefficients is one of the fastest ways to catch a model learning quirks instead of concepts.
The takeaways: build a pipeline, beat a baseline, cross-validate, and inspect the words. Next, we tackle sentiment analysis.
